children: Technology stocks retreated from record highs as strong US activity revived rate-hike fears. Oil, Trump-Xi summit and another test of the AI trade now set the agenda.
Record rally meets the bond market
The Nasdaq Composite
dropped 1.1% Wednesday to 26,936, retreating after two consecutive record closes.
The S&P 500 lost 0.8%, the Dow shed 352 points and the Russell 2000 fell 1.8%, showing that smaller, rate-sensitive companies absorbed the greatest pressure.

September’s US composite PMI climbed to 58.4, its highest since July 2021, signalling faster growth but also stronger inflationary pressure. The 10-year Treasury yield consequently surged above 5.1%, reaching its highest level since 2007.

Early Thursday trading offered little relief. Nasdaq 100 and Dow futures slipped some 0.1% as investors waited for the Trump-Xi meeting. The immediate question is whether Wednesday’s decline was routine profit-taking or the beginning of another valuation adjustment driven by higher bond yields.
Trump and Xi take centre stage

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in Washington Thursday, with an extension of the US-China trade truce at the top of the agenda. AI restrictions, semiconductor exports, supply chains and Taiwan could all influence chipmakers and other technology companies with meaningful Chinese exposure.

Asian markets were cautious before the summit. Japan’s Nikkei jumped more than 1% after reopening from a three-day holiday, but mainland China, Hong Kong and Australia declined. China’s yuan remains near its strongest level in more than three years, reflecting Beijing’s preference for stability around the talks.
Oil complicated the picture by reversing sharply higher. Brent climbed more than 4% toward $104 after Iran’s president rejected US pressure and attached conditions to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Dollar firms as gold and Bitcoin retreat
The dollar advanced toward a two-month high as traders raised the probability of another Fed increase in October to roughly 70%.

Costco reports after Thursday’s closing bell, giving traders a fresh reading on consumer spending and inflation. Consensus estimates point to earnings near $6.55 per share on approximately $94.9 billion in revenue — useful numbers for judging whether the strong economy can tolerate still-higher rates.
